subject: Science
title: Water play
objectives: Children will pour, splash and play with water safely.
Children will say whether things are wet or dry.
content: Pouring and splashing water, deciding whether things are wet or dry, and noticing where water is used in our day.
teachingActivities: Keep water shallow and supervise every moment; use aprons and towels; name each action; let children pour from small jugs; wipe spills at once.
learnerActivities: Pour, splash and play with water safely and say wet or dry.
resources: A cloth and a dry towel
assessment: Observe whether each child pours water safely and says wet or dry for objects.
expectedOutcomes: Pours water from one container to another.
Says wet or dry for objects.

lessons.title: Pouring water
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will pour water from one container to another.
successCriteria: Pours water from a jug into a cup
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children have explored the senses and can describe things as soft, hard, rough and smooth.
lessons.starter: Pour a little water slowly into a cup and say "Pour, pour, pour. Look, the water goes in."
teacherActivities: Show how to hold a jug with two hands and pour slowly into a cup.
Let each child pour water from the jug into a cup while you hold the cup steady.
Ask "Where does the water go?" and "Is the cup full?"
Tip the water back into the basin.
learnerActivities: Children watch and copy holding a jug.
Child pours water into the cup.
Child says or points to where the water went.
Child pours the water back and says "pour".
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show how to hold a jug with two hands and pour slowly into a cup. Children: Children watch and copy holding a jug.
Step 2. Teacher: Let each child pour water from the jug into a cup while you hold the cup steady. Children: Child pours water into the cup.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "Where does the water go?" and "Is the cup full?" Children: Child says or points to where the water went.
Step 4. Teacher: Tip the water back into the basin. Children: Child pours the water back and says "pour".

practical.title: Water pouring
steps: Put on aprons and set up the basin on a waterproof mat.
Each child pours water from a jug to a cup.
practical.safety: Keep water shallow and supervise at all times. Use a waterproof mat and wipe spills at once so no one slips.

differentiation.support: Hold the jug together with the child and pour slowly.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to fill two cups to the top.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

lessons.conclusion: Pour the water back and dry hands with a towel.
lessons.homeConnection: Let your child pour water from a small jug into a cup at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "pour water from one container to another" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

learnerFacing.songOrRhyme: Pour, pour, pour the water. Splash, splash, splash.

lessons.title: Splash and play
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will explore water with their hands and toys and say splash.
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children have explored the senses and can describe things as soft, hard, rough and smooth.
lessons.starter: Tap the water with your hand and say "Splash, splash." Ask "Can you splash?"
teacherActivities: Show how to splash gently with one hand.
Give each child a sponge and show how to squeeze it.
Float plastic toys on the water and say their names.
Say "Stop" and ask children to hold their hands still.
learnerActivities: Children splash gently with a hand.
Child squeezes the sponge and says splash or drip.
Child pushes a toy through the water.
Children stop and watch the water settle.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show how to splash gently with one hand. Children: Children splash gently with a hand.
Step 2. Teacher: Give each child a sponge and show how to squeeze it. Children: Child squeezes the sponge and says splash or drip.
Step 3. Teacher: Float plastic toys on the water and say their names. Children: Child pushes a toy through the water.
Step 4. Teacher: Say "Stop" and ask children to hold their hands still. Children: Children stop and watch the water settle.

practical.title: Splash time
steps: Put on aprons and sit by the basin.
Splash, squeeze and play with toys.
Stop and watch the water settle.
practical.safety: Keep splashing gentle and supervise every child. Wipe the floor often and keep children’s faces dry.

differentiation.support: Play beside the child and move their hand through the water.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to make a big splash and a small splash.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: What do you do with water?

lessons.conclusion: Dry hands and say "Water play is finished."
lessons.homeConnection: Splash gently in the bath or in a bowl of water.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "explore water with their hands and toys and say splash" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Wet and dry
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will say whether objects are wet or dry.
successCriteria: Touches and says wet or dry
Sorts wet and dry things with support
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children have explored the senses and can describe things as soft, hard, rough and smooth.
resources: A wet cloth and a dry cloth
A wet sponge and a dry sponge
lessons.starter: Hold a wet cloth and a dry cloth. Say "This is wet. This is dry." Let children touch both.
teacherActivities: Dip a cloth in water and say "Now it is wet."
Touch a dry towel and say "Dry."
Show pairs of objects and ask "Which is wet?"
Sort wet and dry things into two trays.
learnerActivities: Children touch the wet cloth and say wet.
Children touch the towel and say dry.
Child points to the wet object.
Child puts each object on the correct tray.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Dip a cloth in water and say "Now it is wet." Children: Children touch the wet cloth and say wet.
Step 2. Teacher: Touch a dry towel and say "Dry." Children: Children touch the towel and say dry.
Step 3. Teacher: Show pairs of objects and ask "Which is wet?" Children: Child points to the wet object.
Step 4. Teacher: Sort wet and dry things into two trays. Children: Child puts each object on the correct tray.

practical.title: Wet and dry sort
steps: Put wet and dry objects on the table.
practical.safety: Use only safe objects and wipe up any water. Keep electrical items away from water.

differentiation.support: Touch both objects together and say the word.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to make a dry thing wet and say what happened.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: Is the cloth wet or dry?

expectedOutcomes: Says wet or dry for objects
lessons.conclusion: Hang the wet cloth in the sun and say "It will be dry soon."
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about wet and dry things at home, such as wet clothes and dry towels.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "say whether objects are wet or dry" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Water in my day
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Children will say what we use water for each day.
successCriteria: Names at least two uses of water
Acts out a use of water
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children have explored the senses and can describe things as soft, hard, rough and smooth.
resources: Pictures of drinking, washing, cooking and watering plants
lessons.starter: Show a cup of water and say "We drink water." Pretend to drink.
teacherActivities: Show each picture and say what water is used for.
Act out each use: drink, wash hands, wash a plate, water a plant.
Ask "What do we use water for?" and show the pictures.
Let each child choose a picture and act it.
learnerActivities: Children look and say the use.
Children copy the actions.
Child points to a picture.
Child acts and friends guess.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Show each picture and say what water is used for. Children: Children look and say the use.
Step 2. Teacher: Act out each use: drink, wash hands, wash a plate, water a plant. Children: Children copy the actions.
Step 3. Teacher: Ask "What do we use water for?" and show the pictures. Children: Child points to a picture.
Step 4. Teacher: Let each child choose a picture and act it. Children: Child acts and friends guess.

practical.title: Water uses
steps: Put four pictures on the floor.
Act out each use of water.
practical.safety: Use only clean drinking water for tasting and never allow children to drink from the basin. Supervise closely.

differentiation.support: Offer two pictures and act together.
differentiation.extension: Ask the child to name a use of water at home.

assessment.method: Observe each child during the practical activity and note Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding on the class record. Ask the questions below one to one or in a small group.

questions.question: What else do we use water for?

lessons.conclusion: Say "Thank you, water" and wash hands.
lessons.homeConnection: Talk about how your family uses water each day.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "say what we use water for each day" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?

lessons.title: Week 6 water check
lessons.subject: Science
objectives: Teachers will observe how each child plays with water and uses water words.
lessons.previousKnowledge: Children have explored the senses and can describe things as soft, hard, rough and smooth.
lessons.starter: Sing "Pour, pour, pour the water" and show three stations.
teacherActivities: Set up three stations: pouring, splashing and wet and dry.
At each station ask "What is happening?" and "Is it wet or dry?"
Record each child’s level and take photographs.
learnerActivities: Children rotate every four minutes.
Child answers with a word or action.
Children dry hands and tidy.
presentation: Step 1. Teacher: Set up three stations: pouring, splashing and wet and dry. Children: Children rotate every four minutes.
Step 2. Teacher: At each station ask "What is happening?" and "Is it wet or dry?" Children: Child answers with a word or action.
Step 3. Teacher: Record each child’s level and take photographs. Children: Children dry hands and tidy.

practical.title: Water stations
practical.safety: Supervise each station closely and keep water shallow. Wipe spills quickly.

differentiation.support: Provide an adult partner and use one station.
differentiation.extension: Ask a confident child to explain what they did to a friend.

assessment.method: Observe and record Emerging, Developing, Secure or Exceeding for: pours water; says splash or wet; says wet or dry for objects.

expectedOutcomes: Has an observation record for Week 6
lessons.homeConnection: Let your child help with water tasks at home.
teacherReflection: Which children could show "Teachers will observe how each child plays with water and uses water words" without help, and who needs another turn tomorrow?
What did the children say or do that I did not expect, and how will I use it in the next lesson?
Which resource or instruction worked best, and what would I change before I teach this again?
